After complete-product matching and removal of each product-by-cell mean, relative guide responses remain correlated across the two primary screens. Selecting two guides by their earlier activity shifts the later score by −0.202 log2 units relative to an equal-count randomselection expectation, with negative product-average shifts in 79 of 87 products. Excluding the evaluated cell from the earlier selection score retains a mean shift of −0.192. These results quantify how the history of the intervention can contribute to an apparently repeated phenotype within the observed products and contexts. The underlying principle has clear precedents. JACKS models guide efficacy shared across screens (Allen et al., 2019), library evaluation compares reagent performance (Hart et al., 2017), and current design strategies balance on-target activity and off-target avoidance (Drepanos et al., 2026). Selecting active guides can improve an experiment. Our contribution is the productresolved nORF measurement and the size of its consequence for a later depletion estimate. The worked selection rule is retrospective and is not established to have been used by either source study. Its score shift therefore characterizes a strategy within these data, rather than estimating bias in a particular published validation. The molecular explanation remains open. Greater on-target disruption, sequence-dependent repair, RNA or local regulatory effects and activity at other sites can all contribute to persistent guide responses. Exact-match uniqueness and canonical-CDS avoidance do not exclude mismatch-tolerant off-targets. Copy-number-dependent, gene-independent responses to Cas9 targeting are also documented (Aguirre et al., 2016); our processed endpoints have no newly fitted copy-number correction. Product-by-cell centring removes additive mean responses, but retains multiplicative guide-efficacy differences acting on a true product dependency. Our analytical and synthetic positive control produces both persistent centred responses and a selection shift using only that mechanism (Supplementary Note 5; Figure S3). This compatibility result does not fit or validate an efficacy explanation of the observed data, quantify a technical fraction, or identify which mechanism generates the empirical guide variation. The measurements should therefore be interpreted as intervention responses until a product-specific mechanism is established. Existing nORF biology shows how that attribution can be addressed. Chen et al. (2020) reported initiation-codon-dependent rescue for selected lncRNA- and uORF-encoded products; Prensner et al. (2021) included selected experiments addressing translation-dependent activity. Hofman et al. (2024) linked the medulloblastoma-associated ASNSD1-uORF/ASDURF dependency to the prefoldin-like chaperone complex. Matsumoto et al. (2017) separated SPAR polypeptide loss from expression of its host lncRNA, while D’Lima et al. (2017) connected No- Body to the decapping complex and P-body abundance. The calcium-regulatory activities of myoregulin and DWORF provide further defined mechanisms in mouse muscle (Anderson et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2016). These studies supply evidence beyond pooled-score correspondence. Our reanalysis concerns the repeated perturbation component and does not reassess all source experiments supporting individual examples. Complete-product correspondence is an additional requirement. Initiation mapping and ORFcalling methods distinguish products that a host-gene label alone cannot resolve (Lee et al., 2012; Fields et al., 2015). Annotation guidance provides a shared vocabulary (Mudge et al., 2022), while evolutionary reconstruction and interaction mapping contribute different informa- 15 tion (Vakirlis et al., 2022; Sandmann et al., 2023). Our 274 relationships were constructed from literal source-gene identity or coding-body overlap; 127 match the complete coding chain and DNA. Those counts describe the comparison made here and should not be read as claims originally made by the source authors. The released product and guide tables allow the units of a cross-study comparison to be inspected directly. Translation, stable protein detection and phenotype attribution also require distinct measurements. BAG6-associated triage can direct products of noncoding translation towards degradation or membrane targeting (Kesner et al., 2023), and microprotein mass-spectrometry benchmarking highlights variation in identification support (Wacholder et al., 2026). Cancer immunopeptidomics identifies another relevant output: presentation of noncanonical peptides (Chong et al., 2020; Ouspenskaia et al., 2022), with differences between proteome and immunopeptidome detection (Ruiz Cuevas et al. 2021). Antitumour vaccination responses to selected tumour-specific antigens have been demonstrated in mice (Laumont et al., 2018). Presentation and immune recognition need not require a stable protein or a fitness dependency. Consequently, screen agreement informs functional prioritization while therapeutic targeting also needs evidence appropriate to the proposed modality. The product-level comparisons limit how broadly the selection result can be generalized. In the separate 88-product reused/fresh cohort, balancing guide counts reduces the agreement gap to 0.086, with an interval spanning −0.094 to 0.268. This uncertainty supports neither a general reuse advantage nor equivalence. The conditional guide analysis and the product-level comparison ask different questions. The third publication adds positive aggregate ranking agreement across 196 exact products (Schlesinger et al., 2025), but guide reuse remains unresolved and none reaches its source strong-depletion cutoff. Its product-level Spearman correlation and the conditional within-product Pearson correlations summarize different signals, consistent with the need to match a reproducibility statistic to its intended question (Billmann et al., 2023). A useful cross-study report should specify the complete reference product, exact guide sequences and reuse, how those guides were selected, guide counts, and the outcome being compared. The comparison can then be described as repeated response to shared interventions or agreement obtained with different reagents. Shared-guide evidence remains informative, including in regulatory screens (Yao et al., 2024). To determine molecular attribution, follow-up should connect a defined translated product to the phenotype through complementary interventions, such as rescue and translation-disrupting controls that preserve the relevant RNA. Disease-specific prioritization additionally requires appropriate normal-cell comparisons. Our correspondence resource supports these choices by exposing which products and reagents have actually been compared. The inference is conditional on selected products, published measurements and fixed cancercell contexts. The analysis developed retrospectively; intervals are nominal and do not account for selection across the entire research program. The context-exclusion extension uses already observed cells, and its guide pairs can differ between evaluations. The additional assay is drawn from the earlier study, while the third publication lacks retrieved guide-resolved outcomes. Source baselines, normalization and product summaries differ. Computational reexpression checks numerical consistency; substantive scientific review and complementary experiments remain necessary. Within these limits, the study supplies a reproducible quantitative account of persistent guide responses and the transferable effect of guide selection in matched nORF screens. 16 Generative AI disclosure OpenAI Codex agents contributed substantially to source discovery, literature synthesis, and mathematical exposition Data availability The accompanying Supplementary Data and Code archive contains complete product and guide correspondence inventories, eligibility and exclusion records, all analytical outcomes, fixed protocols, figure-source data and reproduction scripts. paper-19: Experimental context limits transfer of microprotein sequence scores Robin Gounder1, Samuel Schmidt2,3 1University of Cambridge 2Vaionex Corporation 3Cornell University Correspondence: robin@gounder.com Samuel Schmidt: samuel@vaionex.com 10 November 2026 Abstract Sequence scores offer a way to prioritize microproteins encoded by noncanonical open reading frames and propose edits that alter their accumulation. We reanalysed published measurements to test whether these scores remain useful across reporter contexts, independent peptide datasets and paired sequence edits. Among 1,072 development constructs, an annotation-based composition score correlated negatively with reporter accumulation (Spearman ρ = −0.292), whereas models trained on accumulation reached 0.747 using composition and 0.780 with a richer terminal-aware representation. On the same 1,044 peptides across reporters, the within-GFP advantage of the richer representation was uncertain (∆ρ = 0.021, conditional 95% interval −0.005 to 0.046). When applied to microprotein–mCherry, the GFP-trained richer model reached ρ = 0.560, compared with 0.663 for composition alone and 0.742 for a model trained on the target reporter. The paired composition-minus-richer contrast was 0.103 (conditional 95% interval 0.078 to 0.132). Tests on independent canonical peptides and 1,743 paired sequence changes showed that model comparisons also depended on input coverage, training exposure and whether the task was ranking peptides, selecting a subset or predicting edit effects. Strong published baselines reduced several apparent advantages. These retrospective benchmarks quantify predictive portability within the tested populations; they do not isolate causal effects of reporter components. Performance in one reporter does not justify sequence editing or use in another assay without testing. Native turnover and peptide-dependent function require separate experiments. Keywords: microproteins; noncanonical open reading frames; protein stability; sequence predictors; reporter assays; cross-assay transfer; reproducibility 1 1 Introduction Thousands of translated open reading frames fall outside conventional protein annotations, creating a large set of candidate microproteins [1,2]. We refer to these as noncanonical ORFs (nORFs); canonical proteins are those encoded by conventionally annotated coding genes. Sequence scores can help prioritize these candidates, but deciding which peptide to study requires clarity about what a score predicts. Translation, accumulation of a peptide product and peptide-dependent function are different observations. Some noncanonical peptides have established cellular phenotypes or native complex structures [3–5]; an upstream ORF can also affect downstream expression through its RNA or the act of translation [6]. Endogenous-variant and degron-exposure experiments illustrate how particular biological effects can be tested [7,8]. Existing predictors address different parts of this problem. ShortStop classifies sequences by resemblance to curated microproteins relative to synthetic references [27]. PepScore integrates ORF features and was accompanied by individual expression assays [28]. Recent preprints distinguish support from ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry, or predict detection in MS repositories using translation, conservation and peptide attributes [29,30]. These are useful but distinct tasks. A score for annotation resemblance or detection is not automatically a predictor of how much peptide accumulates in a reporter assay. Testing such a score also requires the inputs expected by the original model, including native RNA context where applicable. This distinction also matters when interpreting sequence features. The six-feature XGBoost nORF Score showed no significant association with EggNOG Gene Ontology annotation [9]. Our controlled reanalysis retained compositional differences after exact length matching. Detecting such differences between annotated and noncanonical sequences, however, does not show that the same features predict reporter accumulation or the effect of editing a particular peptide. Those claims require tests against the corresponding measurements. For predicting accumulation, published degradation models provide more direct comparators. These models score degrons: sequences that can direct a protein toward degradation. QCDPred predicts yeast quality-control degrons from composition, with companion experiments on human reporters [10,11]; composition-based methods also support internal degron mapping [12]. Guo et al. studied composition, genetic-code and GC biases, disorder and terminal residues using microprotein reporters, substitutions, extensions and paired reporter configurations [13]. The core assays fuse microproteins to fluorescent reporter proteins and measure the resulting signal. Fusions and tags can change which peptide termini are exposed, making construct context a plausible reason for differences between assays. Cytosolic degron maps and terminal stability screens provide the released peptide abundance predictor (PAP) and DEGRONOPEDIA models [14,18–20]. C-terminal variation and composition-preserving shuffles have also been studied [15, 16], alongside the role of GC constraints in newly evolved sequences [17]. Thus, the importance of composition and sequence context is already established. The practical question is how reliably a score trained in one of these settings can be used in another. Calibration introduces a related question: does a better numerical fit reflect improved prediction, a change in measurement scale or a biological relationship? Experiment-specific nonlinear calibration and variable gains from added features are documented [21]. MAVE-NN and MoCHI model genotype–phenotype and measurement relationships, while recognizing limits on separating their nonlinearities [22,23]. Joint abundance–binding and abundance–activation models [24, 25], and experimentally tested multi-mutant improvements [26], further show why predictive accuracy, physical interpretation and function must be evaluated separately. 2 We ask whether a score that predicts reporter accumulation in one setting remains useful with another reporter or for choosing sequence edits. We first compare annotation-based scores with models trained on reporter measurements. We then hold peptide identity fixed to test prediction across reporter contexts, before testing independent canonical-peptide and pairededit datasets. Comparisons with strong published models, identical sequence inputs and checks for overlap with training data help explain apparent differences in performance. This provides a controlled account of when the tested scores remain useful and where they fail. The later analyses were developed retrospectively after earlier results were known; detailed exploratory results and candidate follow-up remain in S1 Text. Our related guide-selection analysis quantified how earlier CRISPR reagent choices change later depletion estimates [61]. Some ORFs, reference resources and biological precedents are shared with that work. Here the primary measurements are reporter accumulation and paired sequence changes, and the endpoints are predictive portability, input coverage and training exposure; we do not repeat its guide-selection estimands. The contribution is a peptide-matched benchmark of these predictions and their limits, rather than a new reporter experiment or evidence of native peptide function. 2 Results We organize the analyses around the same practical question: when does a score remain useful outside the setting in which it was trained? The core benchmark tests whether training on reporter measurements improves prediction over annotation-based scores. We then ask whether that accuracy survives a change of reporter, a change of study or a change from ranking peptides to predicting edits. Finally, we examine how peptide selection, sequence inputs and training overlap affect the comparisons. All analyses use existing data. The later analyses were developed after earlier results were known and were not preregistered or designed as prospective confirmation. S1 Text contains the detailed results, sensitivity analyses and exploratory candidate checks. 2.1 Training on the measured outcome improves reporter prediction We first asked whether a sequence score trained to recognize annotated proteins also predicts reporter accumulation. To separate the training task from the sequence features, we compared annotation-based scores with models trained on the reporter measurements. Model A uses length and amino-acid composition, T adds terminal features, and O adds residue-order features; all use the same grouped validation folds. Among the 1,072 development constructs, the composition score trained to distinguish annotated proteins from reference sequences correlated negatively with the GFP–microprotein reporter outcome (ρ = −0.292, 95% conditional interval −0.344 to −0.237). ShortStop’s mean SAM probability showed little rank correlation among peptides with available scores (ρ = −0.018; n = 1, 057). Models trained on the measured outcome performed substantially better: composition model A reached ρ = 0.747, and terminal-aware T reached 0.780 (Fig 1; Table 1). The composition model also predicted reporter scores in the additional library after the strict exclusions (ρ = 0.719). A score that distinguishes annotated proteins from reference sequences therefore need not predict reporter accumulation. Two exploratory analyses examine the implications: a separate expression panel tests a further assay change, and sequence matching identifies peptides for experimental follow-up. The scores failed to predict expression in the separate, selected FLAG panel: primary MP– mCherry-trained T had ρ = −0.652 on the strict 20 constructs. Because the panel was selected and used different constructs and an expression-detection assay, this result cannot estimate failure across all microproteins. All model/representation sensitivities, within-study edit analyses and conditional-order controls remain available in S1 Text and Figs S3–S6. Matching full peptide sequences across studies identified three candidates for follow-up: RP11- 620J15.3, JHDM1D-AS1 and the SLCO5A1 uORF peptide. Their existing Leu-to-Ala and append measurements increased reporter output in both source replicates, and the original 9 study reports interaction-tile annotations for their WT sequences [13, 33]. These matches do not show how either edit affects binding, native protein turnover or peptide-dependent activity. S1 Text and S12–S18 Data retain all 60 candidates, the source-reported positive and negative results, the reassessment of native evidence and the limits imposed by RNA context. 3 Discussion 3.1 Transfer depends on the experimental question A microprotein sequence score can perform well in one assay and less well in another. Its usefulness depends on what it was trained to predict, how the peptide was measured and how the score will be used. Composition can distinguish the reference populations studied here and predict reporter accumulation when trained on those measurements. Resemblance to annotated proteins alone does not reliably predict accumulation across assays. Terminal features, calibration and residue order improve prediction in some settings, but no representation performs best in every comparison. The peptides chosen for evaluation can change the conclusion even when the predictions remain fixed. The pooled terminal-feature advantage for Leu-to-Ala effects disappears under the original source exclusion, whereas the append contrast remains positive [13]. The result from all pairs therefore does not apply equally to the subset defined by the original exclusion rule, and it does not explain the molecular cause of the difference. The intended use of the score also matters: GFP-trained T selects a higher-scoring top decile on canonical tiles despite its slightly lower overall correlation. Ranking unmodified peptides, selecting a subset and predicting an intervention are separate tests. Guo et al. already measured both reporter orientations, terminal-degron effects and sequence edits, and supplied predictive models [13]. Our contribution is the grouped, peptide-matched prediction comparison and its extension to edit effects, matched inputs and development exposure. Larsen et al. compared 8,645 common nuclear and cytosolic tiles, finding strong overall agreement alongside terminal-specific exceptions, and applied cytosol-trained PAP to the nuclear screen [41]. Context changes therefore need not impair prediction: portability must be measured for the particular construct, population and decision task. The matched-peptide analysis extends these existing reporter and same-sequence context comparisons. Using identical peptides rules out differences in peptide composition between the tested sets, but reporter identity, orientation and library conditions still change together; MP–mCherry also has a variable-length GS linker and an HA tag. The comparison shows how prediction changes across contexts but cannot identify which construct component causes the change. The selected FLAG-expression panel provides another example of failed prediction across assays. Its selection, construct design and expression-detection readout prevent us from generalizing the failure rate to all microproteins [28]. 3.2 Input coverage and provenance shape predictor comparisons Comparison with strong published models reduces the apparent benefit of calibration. Calibrating linear PAP on source WT measurements improves its predictions of sequence changes, but uncalibrated nonlinear PAP performs better on the same independent pairs. For the full58 neural model, the interval for the additional calibration gain spans zero. Using the full58 input 10 rather than C30 is associated with a much larger improvement. Full58 inference extrapolates beyond the training length, and this contrast does not identify a biological cause. Claims about improved calibration therefore need comparisons that account for both model architecture and the sequence supplied to each model. Experiment-specific nonlinear readouts and separation of measurement from latent biological maps are established methods [21–23]. Interpreting a fitted score as a physical quantity requires independent measurements: Salinas and Ranganathan used affinity-characterized mutants and WT-affinity corrections, while their homologue comparison retained a hypothesized internalequilibrium mechanism [42]. Joint folding/binding and abundance/activity models have their own physical assumptions and validation targets [24, 25]. Higher-order prediction and domainextension or ligand maps also use distinct proteins, substitutions and validation settings [43–45]. Our calibration uses source WT reporter measurements, without an independent molecular measurement. It therefore does not convert reporter scores into a physical stability scale that applies across assays. A test is independent only to the extent that its sequences and related training records have been excluded. The terminal-model audit identifies a smaller set of pairs without known development-screen overlap. Comparing identical C23 inputs also removes most of the apparent performance gap between that model and CNN1. Intervals spanning zero demonstrate neither equivalence nor a universal winner. Higher correlations after exclusions do not establish that exposure caused inflation. Population and decision-metric effects have precedents [26, 46]; our contribution is to compare the models on the same defined peptide sets and provide the records needed to inspect their source and training overlap. Likewise, the small property-feature increment cannot be generalized to all order-aware models. CNN7 retains an order increment on its source study’s held-out tiles, while independent paired-effect intervals span zero. Model shuffles test conditional predictive information, not the biological effects of physically shuffling a peptide. 3.3 Reporter prediction and native function require different evidence Sequence descriptors alone do not identify a degradation mechanism. Composition-conditioned motif prioritization, degron scrambles and stabilized full-length products already have experimental precedents [11, 12, 15]. Terminal screens distinguish encoded sequence from exposed ends and pathway dependence from total stabilization [19,20]. Recognition, ubiquitination and proteasomal engagement are distinct stages [47], potentially affected by accessibility and partner occupancy [8, 48]. Steady-state accumulation also depends on production: under a simple first-order balance, Pss = s/k, where s is production and k includes degradation and dilution. Determining why a particular peptide accumulates therefore requires measurements of both production and turnover. Annotation, detection and evolutionary origin address further distinct targets [17, 27, 29, 30, 49–51]. A peptide-only reporter test cannot refute a model requiring unavailable native RNA context. HLA presentation, intact-product accumulation and peptide-dependent function also require different evidence [35,36]; absence from a detection dataset or screen does not establish lack of function. The three matched candidates suggest experiments; their effects still need to be tested. Synthetic-peptide interactions need not reproduce native stability, concentration or compartmentalization [33], and the edited products were not tested for binding or activity. Characterized MIEF1-MP70 and MRPL33_65 controls have native structural evidence [4], but neither has a 11 matching primary GFP measurement and edit pair in our linked records. Selected rescue and assembly studies establish functional noncanonical products [3,5,52–54], while abundance and functional readouts can diverge [55,56]. JHDM1D-AS1/DHX15 and RP11-620J15.3 RNA studies do not isolate the nominated peptides [57–59]; the reported DHX15 turnover assay measures DHX15 rather than JHDM1D-AS1 peptide clearance. Tests of RNA architecture, translation and released-peptide activity require controls tailored to the candidate [6,28,60]. 3.4 Practical implications To predict reporter accumulation, test the score against measurements from the relevant assay and construct. Scores for annotation resemblance or peptide detection answer different questions and cannot be substituted without testing. When comparing models across studies, specify the sequence given to each model and check for overlap with its training data. Compare strong published models on the same eligible peptides. Report how many peptides receive scores and whether the score is being evaluated for overall ranking or for selecting a subset. Before using a score to choose sequence edits, test whether it predicts measured changes between WT and edited peptides in the relevant population. Higher reporter output does not by itself show slower native turnover or preserved activity. Those claims require assays that can measure both the original and edited products, together with production, turnover and functional tests. 3.5 Limitations and next experiments Several extensions were retrospective and developed after earlier results were known. We use aggregate assay releases, operational dependence groups and intervals conditional on fitted models, rather than raw-data reconstruction, exhaustive remote-homology control or full retraining. Historical training snapshots are incomplete, and post-hoc intervals are not multiplicity-adjusted discovery tests. Canonical tiles independently test our models trained on the source data, but their PAP-development provenance prevents treating the accompanying PAP scores as independent validation of PAP. The three-row paper/release discrepancy is recorded. The common paired cohort audits source/PAP genes and windows, without certifying independence for every predictor. The terminal-model audit lacks individual split membership, does not resolve every alias or remote homologue, and does not audit N-terminal exposure. Comparisons must retain these coverage and provenance limits. Our literature review focused on the claims made in this paper and cannot establish that no earlier study reached a similar conclusion. Native validation should first identify the intact or processed product with an edit-compatible measurement and distinguish production from clearance. WT, the individual edits and the unmeasured combined edit/append panel should be tested separately. Binding or activity should be compared across overlapping measured protein amounts, with a predefined equivalence criterion for preservation. RNA, translation and recoded-peptide rescue controls should separate transcript, translation-process and peptide-sequence explanations. A masking hypothesis additionally requires a validated partner perturbation and a clearance measurement. These experiments could show whether the edits change native turnover, binding or activity. The present work identifies candidates for those tests and shows where predictions remain accurate or fail across the assays examined. 12 4 Conclusions Before using a microprotein sequence score to select peptides or design sequence edits, test whether it predicts the relevant experimental outcome. Composition-based models predict reporter measurements across several settings, but the benefit of terminal features, calibration and residue order depends on the training data, sequence input and assay. Apparent improvements must be compared with strong published models using matched inputs and checks for overlap with training data. Matching peptide sequences across studies also identifies candidates for experiments that distinguish changes in production, turnover, binding and activity. These results show when scores remain useful across the tested assays and when they fail. The effects of the proposed edits on native peptide function remain untested. 5 Materials and methods 5.1 Analysis hierarchy The core benchmark evaluates reporter prediction while keeping related peptides in the same validation group. The later analyses test identical peptides across reporter contexts, independent canonical tiles and paired sequence changes. These analyses address the main question of this paper, but they were developed retrospectively after earlier results were known. Population exclusions, input and training-overlap checks, order and calibration sensitivity analyses, the selected FLAG panel and candidate matching are secondary or exploratory analyses. This hierarchy describes their role in the paper; it does not imply preregistration or prospective confirmation. S1 Text reports all outcomes, including failed prediction across contexts. 5.2 Controlled catalogue context and clustering reproduction To check whether catalogue-level sequence differences persist after controlling for length and GC content, the controlled catalogue analysis reconstructed 28,359 TransCODE Phase 2 candidates against hg38, audited current GENCODE v50 coding overlap and retained 27,670 eligible nORFs. Canonical representatives were the longest valid translated isoform per gene (19,563 genes). The protr descriptor definitions were versioned [31]. Default lag/lambda 30 restricted the all-family comparison to proteins of at least 31 residues; no missing long-lag features were imputed. Exact full-protein length matching after dependence filtering yielded 744 comprehensive pairs, 245 Primary pairs and 472 pairs with an additional absolute GC caliper of 0.02. Matched pairs and linked sequence/gene groups stayed in the same evaluation fold. Clustering used the 1,488 comprehensive matched sequences, all 1,440 descriptors, equalfeature or equal-family weighting, PCA retaining 50 components, k = 2, 3, 5, 8, multiple seeds and 80% subsampling. Native sequences were compared with composition-preserving shuffles. A separate computational rerun checked saved PCA memberships and two t-SNE maps. This reproduces the controlled computation; the original cluster memberships could not be recovered. UMAP was not rerun. The original matrix and complete historical settings remain unavailable. 5.3 Experimental sources and target definitions We used the Guo data because they contain reporter measurements, paired reporter contexts and measured sequence edits. This lets us test different uses of a score while retaining exact sequence 13 and parent links. The Guo supplementary tables supply normalized fusion-reporter scores [13]. The primary development set comprises 1,072 valid wild-type (WT) GFP–microprotein (GFP– MP) cargos; 1,071 have both reported biological replicates. The opposite MP–mCherry orientation supplies 1,046 measured WTs. A separate GFP–MP mutagenesis library contains 1,072 WT baselines, 730 HLA-associated and 71 digest-MS-associated natural sequences, and engineered variants. The additional 801 sequences are absent as exact peptides from the released 1,072-row Guo regression-training table. They remain within the same study, and their availability does not establish prospective blinding of the published models. We used released means, available biological replicate cells, oligos and source-code metadata. The publisher’s article-plus-supplement file subsequently provided full STAR Methods access [13]. The source describes within-bin counts-per-million normalization, five bin weights (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9), their counts-weighted average and replicate-specific min–max scaling. We did not rerun that raw read processing or infer censoring from aggregate scores. Raw read-depth and censoring information were not obtained for this reanalysis. These limitations constrain error and detection interpretation. Throughout, “reporter score” denotes the supplied assay measurement, not an endogenous half-life, thermodynamic folding stability or function. Exact sequence editing verified 1,014 global Leu-to-Ala pairs and 1,007 extensions by the constant C-terminal sequence DNYNEPKANQ. Observed change was mutant minus WT score in the same mutagenesis library. Original and mutagenesis-library WT measurements differ, so the former were not substituted as mutant baselines. Missing outcomes or predictors were not replaced by zero. These all-sequence-valid populations are broader than the source’s specified Leu-to-Ala analysis: its STAR Methods exclude WTs containing Leu at either of the last two residues, and Fig. 4F states this restriction for the WT/substitution/extension comparison [13]. After recovering the full methods, we applied that WT-sequence rule to both edit families as a post-hoc sensitivity, retaining all earlier fits and predictions. This retained 798 Leu-to-Ala pairs in 611 operational groups and 802 append pairs in 623 groups. All, retained and omitted strata, mean and both replicate effects, all 20 original predictors and compatible-scale errors are supplied in S12 Data. T-minus-A, O-minus-T and calibrated-minus-raw full-PAP rank contrasts use 1,000 group resamples conditional on the original fits, with no multiplicity adjustment. An independent workbook reader checked all 2,021 membership flags; an independent rank implementation checked 360 point metrics and 18 point contrasts. Bootstrap distributions were not independently replayed. This changes the evaluation population, not the fitted models, and does not reproduce every original assay-processing decision. The separate Yang assay contains 29 uORFs and eight other ORFs, with native lengths 17–129 residues [28]. We translated all 37 supplied synthesized constructs, verified their reported lengths and terminal DYKDDDDK FLAG tags, and joined measurements by ORF name. Untreated outcomes are the mean of five replicates for the 29 uORFs and four for the other eight. The target is GFP-normalized FLAG-positive cell fraction, not the Guo numerical scale. The source describes the 29 uORFs as randomly selected across PepScores; the eight other ORFs were chosen with high scores. The combined 37-construct set mixes these selection schemes and ORF classes; it is not a population-wide validation sample. 5.4 Dependence audit and score provenance We grouped records linked by identical peptide sequences, a shared parental construct, available gene identities or overlapping catalogue entries. Engineered sequences shared by different par- 14 ents connected those parents. We exhaustively aligned eligible pairs among native assay peptides, Yang natives, annotation-reference sequences and available ShortStop positive-reference counterparts. Local Smith–Waterman alignment used BLOSUM62, gap-open 10 and gap-extension 1. Primary edges required at least 60% identity over alignment columns and at least 80% coverage of both full sequences; a 40% identity graph was a declared sensitivity. Length and composition bounds only removed pairs that could not meet these criteria. Connected components defined split groups. These groups keep known linked records together during validation. They do not rule out distant homology or earlier exposure during pretraining. The annotation-trained AAC classifier retained the original fixed Extra Trees configuration: 200 trees, maximum depth 10, minimum leaf 10, square-root feature sampling, balanced classes and seed 100. Whole reference pairs and linked reference split groups were removed to a fixed point if connected to any Guo or Yang parent. Seeds 101 and 102 were sensitivity analyses. Higher scores indicate canonical resemblance, opposite to the nORF Score convention [9]; this classifier was not trained on reporter measurements. ShortStop v1.2.0 (28 October 2026) precomputed scores were joined only after independent GTF translation against hg38 verified exact peptide identity. The primary continuous score was mean SAM probability across released models. Published standard and stringent consensus calls were retained as distinct threshold analyses. Actual supervised-positive identifiers were distinguished from ToBePredicted records, which the inspected training code excludes from supervision. The 1,571 available positive-reference sequences are from the current reviewed release, which does not provide a complete archive of historical training sequences. Thus absence of exact matches does not establish complete training or pretraining separation. The frozen PAP human30 model was reimplemented from safely parsed published numeric coefficients [14]. Primary transfer uses the final min(30, L) residues. Composition terms scale residue counts to 30 positions; terminal, pair and triplet terms follow the released positional definition. The full-peptide version uses normalized composition and is evaluated as a secondary analysis; PAP was not refitted. Deposited Guo classification/regression predictions were evaluated only on the additional natural sequences and their strict subset, not against other methods’ held-out predictions on Guo’s own training rows. Supplied PepScore values were used only for the exact Yang constructs; unavailable transcript, domain and evolutionary inputs were left missing. 5.5 Endpoint models, order controls and nested validation To evaluate predictions on peptides whose related records were absent from training, models used five outer and three inner group folds. Groups were randomly tie-broken with seed 20261031, sorted by descending size and greedily assigned to the smallest fold without using outcomes.
